status_summary: Executive Order 14266 (2025-04-09) raised duties on low-value shipments from China as part of closing de minimis treatment for China, and Executive Order 14324 (signed 2025-07-30) suspended duty-free de minimis treatment for all countries effective 2025-08-29, which goes beyond the China-focused recommendation. Executive Order 14388 (2026-02-20) kept the suspension in force after the Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA tariffs, Executive Order 14389 states that the suspension is unaffected by its ending of IEEPA duties, and on 2026-08-13 the Court of International Trade, in Axle of Dearborn v. Department of Commerce (Slip Op. 26-94), granted the government summary judgment on the challenges to the presidential rescission of de minimis treatment and to its agency implementation, while deferring judgment on a separate count about refunds of IEEPA duties. CBP implemented an indefinite suspension by interim final rules of 2026-06-24, and on 2026-10-22 it moved the compliance date for formal entry of certain postal shipments to 2027-01-20 without changing the suspension. Public Law 119-21 (Section 70531) modifies the statutory de minimis privilege: per the amendment notes on the U.S. Code page for 19 U.S.C. 1321, it adds a civil penalty provision (effective 30 days after enactment) and, effective 2027-07-01, strikes the $800 category for other shipments and the civil penalty provision, leaving the exemptions for bona fide gifts and for articles accompanying arriving persons; CBP's proposed rule of 2026-10-08 states that the statutory exemption ends 2027-07-01.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14266 raises duties on low-value shipments from China (ad valorem rate from 90 to 120 percent and per-item fee from $75 to $100 on 2025-05-02, then $200 on 2025-06-01), part of the closure of de minimis treatment for China.
Public Law 119-21 enacted; its table of contents lists Section 70531 on modifications to the de minimis entry privilege for commercial shipments.

Section 70531 of Public Law 119-21 is enacted. Per the amendment notes on the U.S. Code page for 19 U.S.C. 1321, subsection (a) adds a civil penalty provision ($5,000 for a first violation, $10,000 for each later one) effective 30 days after enactment, and subsection (b), effective 2027-07-01, strikes the $800 category for other shipments from subsection (a)(2) and strikes the civil penalty provision, leaving the exemptions for bona fide gifts and for articles accompanying arriving persons.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14324, Suspending Duty-Free De Minimis Treatment for All Countries, is signed (2025-07-30); the suspension takes effect 2025-08-29 at 12:01 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time.
Executive Order 14388 amends Executive Order 14324 to keep the suspension for all countries, effective 2026-02-24, with postal duties collected at the Section 122 surcharge rate.
Supreme Court holds IEEPA does not authorize tariffs; Executive Order 14389 states the de minimis suspension order is not affected by its ending of IEEPA duties.

The Court of International Trade (Axle of Dearborn v. Department of Commerce, Slip Op. 26-94, Court No. 25-00091, per curiam) holds that the emergency-powers statute (IEEPA) authorizes the President to rescind the de minimis exemption, which it treats as a statutory privilege; treats agency implementation as ministerial and not reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act; grants the government summary judgment on Counts I-II and denies as moot its motion to dismiss Count II; and defers judgment on Count III, which concerns refunds of IEEPA duties.

CBP proposes a rule on low-value shipments (91 FR 64532; comments due 2026-12-07) requiring informal entries of goods valued at 2,500 dollars or less to be filed electronically at or before importation, creating an informal mail entry type with tracking-number data, requiring a licensed broker for some consignees and an entry bond, and allowing blanket formal-entry requirements. It cites Executive Orders 14324 and 14388 on the de minimis suspension and states that the 2025 reconciliation law ends the de minimis exemption effective 2027-07-01.

CBP publishes a final rule (91 FR 66638, RIN 1685-AA45), issued without notice and comment under the good-cause exception, extending the compliance date for formal entry of postal shipments subject to partner agency requirements, Chapter 98 or 99 duties, or certain duty-free claims under 19 CFR 145.12(a)(2)(v) and (vi) from 2026-10-22 to 2027-01-20; the de minimis suspension and the informal postal entry process from the 2026-06-24 interim final rule (91 FR 37801) stay in place.

title: End the de minimis exemption that lets low-value Chinese shipments avoid tariffs
uncertainties: The 2027-07-01 statutory end date is stated in CBP's 2026-10-08 proposed rule and reported by Alvarez & Marsal, and the amendment notes on the law.cornell.edu U.S. Code page for 19 U.S.C. 1321 (read 2026-10-22) cite section 70531(b) and the same effective date. The govinfo.gov text of Public Law 119-21 could not be read as far as section 70531, so the section's own wording was not read; the Code page still prints the pre-amendment text of subsection (a)(2) and the civil penalty subsection because the subsection (b) amendments are not yet effective. The Code notes show no country limitation; an external retrieval of the enrolled text also reports none, which was not verified against an opened copy. The 2025-08-29 start of the global suspension rests on the order text and Federal Register records. Executive Order 14256 (2025-04-02), which earlier record text describes as ending duty-free de minimis treatment for goods from China effective 2025-05-02, was not read; the China-specific steps rest on Executive Order 14266. The 2026-06-24 interim final rules were not read directly; they are known through the 2026-10-22 final rule, which cites 91 FR 37801, and the Alvarez & Marsal report. The 2026-10-22 final rule was read through a summary of its Federal Register page; it cites 19 U.S.C. 1321 and Executive Orders 14324 and 14388 but not Public Law 119-21. The Court of International Trade's opinion of 2026-08-13 was opened and read on the court's site (cit.uscourts.gov); the slip-opinion number field appeared blank in the text read, so the number 26-94 rests on the court's file name and the Alvarez & Marsal report. The opinion grants the government summary judgment on Counts I-II and defers Count III, so it is not a final judgment on all counts. No appeal of the de minimis rulings was found (a negative search result); the opinion cites a separate Federal Circuit appeal (No. 26-1895, V.O.S. Selections) concerning a liquidation order in another case.
